personality_voice.book_baseline: Arthur Weasley is defined by a cluster of deeply consistent traits across all seven books: genuine, almost childlike enthusiasm for Muggle objects and culture ('Fascinating. Ingenious, really, how many ways Muggles have found of getting along without magic'); warm, inclusive, slightly bumbling fatherliness; a cheerful willingness to bend rules he helped write (the Invisibility Booster, the loophole in the Muggle car law); mild-mannered conflict avoidance that occasionally gives way to real, physical anger when his family or values are threatened (the fight with Lucius at Flourish and Blotts); earnest professionalism at the Ministry despite his lowly status; and a capacity for genuine moral seriousness when stakes are high (his warning to Harry about Black, his concern about Muggle-baiting, his rebuke to Fred and George about the Engorgement Toffee). His speech is warm, slightly flustered, prone to enthusiastic tangents, and punctuated by genuine paternal anxiety. He is never pompous, rarely sarcastic, and his anger, when it appears, is hot and principled rather than cold.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the core of this personality very well. Mark Williams's performance captures the Muggle enthusiasm ('Excellent!' at the campsite, delighting in the ticket machines and the Underground, asking Harry about parking meters), the warm paternal inclusiveness (embracing Harry, toasting Harry at Christmas in OotP), the principled anger (the confrontation with Lucius in Chamber is present, though he is restrained by Hagrid rather than physically launching himself), and the slight flustered quality in his speech. The Leaky Cauldron warning to Harry in PoA is faithful in tone and content. The OotP dinner scene and his Christmas toast ('To Harry Potter, without whom I would not be here') add a warmth fully in keeping with the books.
personality_voice.difference: Several important vocal and behavioral textures are thinned. The books show Arthur's speech in much greater detail across sustained sequences: his running Ministry commentary at the World Cup campfire, his extended Muggle enthusiasm on the Underground in OotP, his earnest back-and-forth with Perkins, his fumbling with Muggle money at the campsite. The films preserve the highlights but collapse much of the texture. His rule-bending contradiction (building the Invisibility Booster while lecturing about Muggle protection) is present but reduced. His anger at Fred and George over the Engorgement Toffee—one of his most revealing moments of principled fury—is cut from CoS; the film shows the aftermath via Howler only. The PoA overheard argument (Arthur fighting Molly to tell Harry the truth about Black) is significantly condensed in the film to a brief, more surface-level warning scene.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The personality is recognizably and substantially preserved. The reduction is in texture and secondary moments rather than in core traits. A minor penalty is warranted for the loss of the Engorgement Toffee confrontation (which shows Arthur's principled anger beyond his family-vs-Malfoy mode), the collapse of sustained Muggle-enthusiasm sequences, and the thinning of his speech patterns across PoA and GoF. These do not alter the character's identity but do reduce its richness. Score sits in the 18-22 range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Arthur Weasley serves multiple structural functions across the series: (1) a conduit for plot-critical information (warning Harry about Black in PoA, reporting on the Ministry's infiltration in OotP, relaying intelligence about Death Eater movements in HBP and DH); (2) a moral compass for the adult wizarding world—the books repeatedly contrast his egalitarian values with Lucius Malfoy's pure-blood snobbery; (3) an active participant in Order of the Phoenix operations; (4) the agent who provides access to Ministry-world scenes (the GoF hearing in OotP, the World Cup logistics in GoF); (5) a plot driver in CoS (his enchanted car, his fine, the diary planted by Lucius to undermine his Muggle Protection Act); (6) a victim whose near-death is a major emotional and plot catalyst in OotP. In the books he initiates, decides, warns, confronts, and changes events—he is rarely merely decorative.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: Many of these functions survive. His warning to Harry in PoA is intact and given its own discreet scene at the Leaky Cauldron. His role in the OotP Ministry hearing sequence (escorting Harry, providing emotional reassurance, alerting Harry about the changed schedule) is fully preserved and well-executed. His near-death in OotP retains its plot function. His Patronus message at the wedding ('Family safe, do not reply') is present. His work at the Ministry in DH (being tracked, the lift encounter with Harry-as-Runcorn) is partially preserved in the theatrical cut—the confrontation in the lift where Harry warns him is retained, though the cut scene of Ron staying silent while Harry-as-Runcorn defends Arthur is excluded. He participates visibly in the Battle of Hogwarts and is shown mourning Fred.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several areas of agency are reduced or transferred. In CoS, his role as the implicit target of the diary plot (Lucius planted it to destroy Arthur's Muggle Protection Act) is kept at a summary level in Dumbledore's final exposition but is never dramatized as Arthur's struggle—he is present but passive in the Diagon Alley confrontation compared to the book, where he physically throws himself at Lucius. In OotP, his key function of arguing with Molly about telling Harry the truth (a scene that shows his independent moral judgment and his willingness to defy both his wife and the Ministry's approach) is heavily compressed to a brief corridor exchange in the Leaky Cauldron, removing the extended debate that shows him as an active agent of Harry's protection. In HBP, his role as a Ministry intelligence asset who investigates the Vanishing Cabinet on Harry's behalf (book scenes 1128-1143 and the Christmas Eve conversation in book scene 1149-1168) is preserved in the film's Christmas party scene and is one of the better-adapted moments. The Potterwatch radio scene (book 29 in the film corpus, DH shed scene) is confirmed cut and loses his quiet role building the Order's communication network.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Arthur retains his main structural functions but loses meaningful agency in two key areas: the PoA argument scene (which shows him as a decisive advocate for Harry against institutional inertia) and the CoS physical confrontation (where the film has him restrained rather than initiating). The Potterwatch radio scene, confirmed cut, removes a quiet but significant act of independent initiative. A moderate penalty applies: his role is still recognizable and functional, but some active agency has been either compressed or transferred to passive presence.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Arthur's motivations are layered but consistent: genuine love for Muggles that is both philosophical (they deserve respect and protection) and personal (enthusiastic delight); deep loyalty to his family, which sometimes conflicts with his duty to the Order and to Harry; principled commitment to fairness and anti-discrimination at the Ministry despite this costing him professionally; a suppressed desire to fight back against pure-blood prejudice; and in DH, the specific fear of losing family members combined with a dogged commitment to the cause. His internal conflict is most explicit in PoA, where he genuinely disagrees with Molly about whether to tell Harry the truth—a conflict between protecting Harry emotionally and protecting him practically. He also shows quiet bitterness about his professional situation (the Muggle Protection Act, being passed over, the small windowless office) that he rarely voices directly.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The core motivations are present: Muggle enthusiasm is clearly motivated by genuine affection and philosophical principle (the film preserves his disgust at Muggle-baiting in the Engorgement Toffee scene's aftermath, and his remarks about wizard responsibility at the World Cup). His family loyalty is strongly conveyed, particularly in OotP and DH. His commitment to the Order's cause is clear throughout. The HBP Christmas party scene correctly shows him as someone still working, still sharing intelligence with Harry despite personal risk.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The internal conflict about whether to tell Harry the truth (PoA) is greatly compressed. In the books, this is a sustained, heated argument between Arthur and Molly that reveals his independent moral judgment and his deep respect for Harry's autonomy—he believes Harry has a right to know. In the film, this becomes a brief warning scene in which Arthur simply tells Harry about Black, without the preceding argument revealing why he is doing it against institutional advice. The tension between his professional ethics and his personal affection for Harry (which drives his covert actions throughout OotP) is implied but not dramatized. His quiet bitterness about his professional situation, which in the books provides texture to his motivations, is absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are simplified but recognizably correct. The core drive (family, fairness, Muggle affection, Order loyalty) is intact. The main simplification is the PoA internal conflict, which is compressed from a fully dramatized scene to a brief action. This is a compression that affects characterization somewhat—the film Arthur warns Harry but does not reveal the moral reasoning or the conflict behind doing so. This sits in the 11-13 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Arthur's arc across the series is a gradual movement from a relatively safe, domestically comfortable Ministry employee who bends rules for his hobbies, to someone whose world is dismantled by Voldemort's return—his son nearly dies, his family is endangered, his institution is corrupted, he loses a child. The arc is not one of dramatic internal transformation but of tested endurance: his values are confirmed under pressure rather than changed. Key turning points: his near-death in OotP (which tests his family's resilience and Harry's connection to the Weasleys); Percy's estrangement and reconciliation; Fred's death; and his role in the final battle. By DH, he has become a wartime father doing dangerous underground work while maintaining quiet normalcy for his family.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The broad shape of the arc is present. He begins as a warm, enthusiastic Ministry man; his near-death in OotP has its emotional weight; Percy's estrangement is shown (though compressed); Fred's death is depicted, with Arthur shown comforting Molly; and he fights in the Battle of Hogwarts and is shown alive at the end. The DH shed scene (confirmed cut in theatrical release) would have shown his quiet DH-era transformation most explicitly, but in its absence, his wartime role is conveyed primarily through brief appearances.
character_arc.difference: Several arc steps are compressed or missing. Percy's reconciliation at the Battle of Hogwarts is present but the full weight of the estrangement (Arthur being ignored at the Ministry, the poisonous letter Percy sent, Mrs. Weasley's grief) is not built up sufficiently in the films to give the reconciliation its full impact. The OotP arc—Arthur surviving near-death, the family's vigil, Harry's guilt—is present but the emotional complexity of Arthur's recovery (the Muggle stitches scene at St Mungo's, which shows his incorrigible Muggle curiosity even while injured) is cut. This scene is a genuine arc beat, not mere comedy—it shows that even mortal danger does not change who he fundamentally is.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but retains its major structural beats: rise, testing, loss, endurance. The absence of the St Mungo's stitches scene and the fully dramatized Percy estrangement reduces the arc's texture but does not contradict it. Score in the 11-13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Arthur's most important relationships in the corpus are: (1) Molly—a marriage of genuine warmth with occasional real tension (the PoA argument, the loophole confrontation in CoS, her worry about his Muggle enthusiasm); (2) Harry—Arthur treats Harry as a surrogate son from early in CoS, and this relationship deepens meaningfully through OotP (the Ministry hearing escort, the hospital vigil, the Christmas toast); (3) his children collectively, and Fred and George specifically (his principled anger at their pranks combined with amusement he can barely suppress); (4) Lucius Malfoy—a sustained antagonistic dynamic representing the values conflict at the heart of the series. The books establish the Molly-Arthur marriage as a genuine partnership with friction, not just domestic comedy.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry relationship is well-preserved—the films consistently show Arthur as protective, warm, and genuinely paternal toward Harry, and the OotP hearing escort sequence is one of the better-adapted book-to-film moments. The Lucius antagonism is preserved in CoS and OotP. The Fred/George relationship is shown through brief moments of amused complicity. The Molly-Arthur dynamic is present but flattened: the films show warmth and the 'Mollywobbles' exchange in HBP (a brief intimate moment) but the PoA argument—the most revealing example of their relationship having real friction and genuine disagreement on important matters—is eliminated, replaced by a unilateral decision by Arthur.
key_relationships.difference: The Molly-Arthur relationship loses its most important scene of genuine conflict. In the books, their argument about Harry shows that Arthur's relationship with Molly is one of equals who can disagree profoundly—and that Arthur is not simply her follower. In the films, he acts alone without the context of having fought for Harry's right to know. The Fred/George relationship is also thinner in the films—the book's sustained pattern of Arthur being exasperated yet secretly amused by them (the Engorgement Toffee confrontation that he apparently backs down from with Molly) is compressed.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The most important relationship (Arthur-Harry) is well-preserved. The Molly-Arthur dynamic is meaningfully simplified by the removal of the PoA argument. The Lucius antagonism is retained. Overall the relationships are mostly faithful but the Molly-Arthur depth is reduced. Score in the 7-8 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Arthur's complexity in the books lies in several contradictions: he is a law enforcer who breaks laws; a champion of Muggle protection who endangers Muggles with his enchanted car; a gentle man capable of sudden violent anger; someone whose professional failure (windowless office, low status) is never bitter but is a source of quiet dignity; a father whose warmth includes real principled fury; someone who, in DH, is quietly doing dangerous and important work while maintaining normalcy. The books give him comic moments that also reveal character (Muggle money confusion, Floo powder enthusiasm) and serious moments that reveal moral depth (the PoA argument, defending Winky's innocence, warning Harry about Malfoy). His reaction to Percy's estrangement—silent, controlled pain—is also a significant characterization beat.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films preserve the comic complexity (Muggle enthusiasm is consistently played as both funny and genuine) and the warmth. The principled anger in the Lucius confrontation is present. The OotP and DH material shows him as capable of serious, dangerous work.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Several nuance-rich scenes are absent: (1) The Engorgement Toffee confrontation (CoS), which shows his capacity for genuine principled anger at his own sons and his conflicted relationship with Fred and George's entrepreneurialism; (2) The St Mungo's stitches scene (OotP), which shows his incorrigible character under adversity; (3) The PoA overheard argument, which shows him as someone willing to defy his wife's wishes on a matter of principle; (4) The Potterwatch radio scene (DH, confirmed cut), which shows his quiet, creative contribution to the resistance; (5) The Ministry OotP scenes' full texture—his small windowless office, his running commentary on Ministry colleagues, his dignified response to professional marginalization—is compressed. The film Arthur is slightly more uniformly warm and slightly less contradictory than the book Arthur.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The lost material is real and meaningful—it collectively removes the most interesting edges of his personality (the contradiction between law-enforcer and rule-breaker, the principled anger at his own family, the dignity under professional failure, the quiet agency in wartime). The remaining portrayal is accurate but simplified. This is noticeable simplification of important nuances, placing the score in the 8-10 range.

CoS: Arthur's principled furious confrontation with Fred and George over the Engorgement Toffee (book scene; film shows only Howler aftermath)
CoS: The extended 'loophole' confrontation with Molly over the enchanted car, showing Arthur's self-aware rule-bending humor

OotP: The full texture of Arthur's Ministry office (windowless, littered with Muggle objects, cramped beside Perkins)—showing his dignified endurance of professional marginalization
OotP: The St Mungo's Christmas scene where Arthur attempts Muggle stitching on his snake-bite wounds—showing his incorrigible Muggle enthusiasm even while recovering from near-death
OotP: Arthur's extended running commentary on Ministry colleagues at the World Cup campfire (book GoF scenes), compressed to brief exchanges in the film
DH Part 1: Potterwatch radio scene (confirmed cut)—Arthur quietly building communication radios for Order members on the run, showing wartime agency and initiative

DH Part 1: The full Ministry lift sequence where Arthur confronts Runcorn is retained, but the cut scene of Ron-as-Cattermole staying silent while Harry-as-Runcorn defends Arthur removes additional texture

General: Arthur's sustained Muggle-enthusiasm sequences across multiple films compressed—Underground in OotP, campsite money fumbling in GoF, extended Floo powder explanation in CoS—reduced to highlights rather than full scenes
score_caps_applied: Cap 1 (85): Not triggered—the remaining material is substantially faithful rather than superficially so, and the complexity losses, while real, do not constitute removal of a 'major part' of complexity.
Cap 2 (80): Borderline but not applied—the Molly-Arthur relationship is simplified but not substantially changed; the core dynamic is recognizable.
Cap 3 (75): Not triggered—no single core function, idea, or act of agency is fully transferred to another character; Arthur's main contributions remain his own.
No caps applied—final score of 75 reached organically from dimension scores without requiring cap enforcement.
comparative.key_observations: Arthur Weasley is one of the better-adapted supporting characters in the Harry Potter film series. His core personality—Muggle enthusiasm, warm paternal inclusiveness, principled values, mild-mannered competence with occasional flashes of real anger—is consistently and recognizably present across all eight films. The performances and screenplay selections correctly identify what is most essential about him. The losses are real but concentrated: the PoA overheard argument is the single most significant omission, as it is the scene where Arthur most clearly acts as an independent moral agent against institutional and familial pressure; its compression into a unilateral warning reduces his characterization from principled advocate to dutiful informer. The Engorgement Toffee confrontation and the St Mungo's stitches scene, both cut, together remove the most revealing examples of his contradictory nature. The confirmed-cut Potterwatch radio scene loses his quiet wartime initiative. What remains is an Arthur Weasley who is warm, funny, genuinely Muggle-obsessed, and clearly good—but somewhat less complex, less contradictory, and less agentive than his book counterpart. The score of 75 reflects a faithful but meaningfully simplified adaptation.
